extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novelists and short-story writers) wanting to create immersive settings
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and concrete techniques for creating immersive temporal, environmental, and individual settings in fiction (especially novels), including sensory strategies, integration with plot/character, and common pitfalls to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal setting (era / when)
rubrics_metrics.description: This describes the era in which the story takes place (when the story is set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the reader in the correct time from the start. Rather than just writing a date at the top of the page, use specific details (language, materials, technology, smells, etc.) to show the time (example: Kate Mosse passage evoking Paris 1891). Use temporal sensory cues (e.g., coal and smoke for The Great Smog) to boost period feel; avoid merely labelling time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental setting (geography / larger surroundings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The larger geographical area and surrounding locations where the story takes place (e.g., country, city vs rural, landscape features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose environmental anchors that inform character decisions and expectations (example: Cornwall implies beaches/cliffs/seagulls). You can set in real locations or invented ones, but anchor the reader with familiar physical factors (sea, mountains, forest) so they can picture the place without excessive exposition. Use environmental contrasts to reinforce narrative stakes (e.g., Shire vs Mordor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual setting (specific scene location and details)
rubrics_metrics.description: The nitty-gritty: the particular room, bench, hut, or street where a scene takes place and the small details found there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use detailed, sensory specifics (splinters on a bench, creaking floorboards, scent of flowers) to deepen character emotion and ground scenes. Individual setting is where you can most richly evoke atmosphere and character through tactile, olfactory, auditory, visual, and gustatory details (example: The Mercies excerpt describing heather and scent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use all five senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ smell, hearing, touch, sight, and taste to create a fuller, more immersive setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consciously consider each sense when describing scenes; each sense can heighten different aspects of temporal, environmental, or individual setting. The article recommends breaking techniques down by sense and using them where effective rather than randomly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smell as a period/time cue
rubrics_metrics.description: Use scent to evoke era-specific atmospheres (e.g., coal and smoke indicating a historical London smog).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smell can rapidly place readers in a period or environment because scents are strongly associative. Use olfactory detail to locate readers in a specific time or social/historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing to expand environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sounds (owls, rustling leaves, creaking branches) to enlarge the sense of place and atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auditory details can extend environmental setting and build tension or mood (e.g., night woods), helping readers imagine what the character experiences in that larger landscape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Touch to deepen emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tactile details (smoothness of a rock, splinters) to intensify character feeling and make individual settings vivid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Touch links physical detail to character reaction and memory, reinforcing emotional stakes tied to objects and places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sight to establish environmental features
rubrics_metrics.description: Use visual details (lights, colours, crowds) to paint the larger setting and place the reader in the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sight often carries the initial image of a place—describe what the character sees on entering a space to anchor the scene (example: funfair lights and colours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste to enrich scenes (especially food/sea/physical sensations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use taste not only for food scenes but also to evoke environment (e.g., tang of sea air) or add unsettling detail (e.g., taste of blood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste can be unexpected and striking; using gustatory detail judiciously enhances vividness of individual moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid info dumps
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not spend long stretches of prose describing every aspect of a place in one go (e.g., 'spending five pages describing flowers around a cottage').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern readers favour momentum. Integrate description into action and character experience so setting is learned naturally (example: describe the smell of roses while the character searches for keys, or have another character pluck a flower). Info dumps pull readers out of the story—spread sensory detail through scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don’t tell (concrete detail over labels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than telling the reader a setting or labelling a time/place (e.g., adding a date), show it through specific, grounded details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use particulars of materials, behaviour, language, and sensory cues to indicate place/time. The article explicitly contrasts adding a date with showing period through scene detail; the 'show don't tell' adage underpins effective temporal and environmental setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask fundamental questions about setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a checklist of questions to evaluate what to include: How does the setting initially look? What other senses does it evoke? What does your character think of it? How does it affect the character’s life? How does it mirror their personality or predicament? What aspects are important to mention, and which will take readers away from the action?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions when planning or revising scenes to decide which details to include and how to integrate them into character/action rather than stopping the story for exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting to reinforce theme and mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Make setting serve thematic and tonal purposes (e.g., Shire = comfort/home; Mordor = danger/desolation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose contrasts and recurring environmental imagery to echo and amplify theme, raise stakes, or signal shifts in mood; the page uses Tolkien to show how contrasting landscapes drive the story of good vs evil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting to provide social and character context
rubrics_metrics.description: Let setting supply information about a character’s social environment, background, and likely behaviours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geography and immediate surroundings suggest class, occupation, cultural norms and constraints; this reduces the need for explicit exposition about character backstory and influences believable choices by characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan and plot setting (it takes time and practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating effective setting requires planning, plotting, and practice—don’t expect it to appear fully formed without work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about setting across the manuscript (which places recur, which details matter to plot/themes) and weave sensory and environmental information into story beats rather than treating setting as an afterthought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less is more / subtlety
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting should be subtle and effortless—strong enough to mark the story but not so obvious that it dominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every paragraph needs sensory lists. Use restraint: setting should 'feel so effortless that you have to specifically look for it.' It should highlight character and theme without taking control of the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor invented worlds with familiar cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in invented or fantastic settings, give readers something recognisable or comprehensible to orient them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical factors or analogues (e.g., 'glittering sea', 'thick dark forest') so readers can map your invented locations onto familiar experiences and thus enter the story world quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate description into action and character experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Let readers learn about setting through what characters do, think, and perceive in the moment rather than separate descriptive passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed sensory detail in interactions and movements; use characters’ reactions and tasks to reveal important elements of place so description supports momentum and character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t force all techniques every time (use intuition)
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not have to use every sense or every technique in every paragraph—use your writerly intuition to choose what’s needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat advice as flexible: pick the most effective sensory cues and details for the scene. The author explicitly advises taking advice with a 'pinch of salt' and following your gut about what to include.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise details that matter to plot and reader attention
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which aspects of setting are important to mention and which will distract or slow pace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include setting details that either (a) advance plot, (b) reveal character, or (c) enhance theme/mood. Trim or omit peripheral details that interrupt action or dilute focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make setting the 'silent shining star'—supporting, not overpowering
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting should cushion plot and characters: it supports and polishes the story without drawing attention to itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat setting as an enhancer—enough to make the story 'shine' and stand out on the shelf, but never so obvious that readers notice the setting instead of the story.
